title: Encode String with Shortest Length
statement:
Compress the string `s` of lowercase letters into the shortest possible text. A block written as `k[t]` stands for the text `t` repeated exactly `k` times, where `k` is a positive integer written in decimal and `t` may itself contain blocks; a letter outside any block stands for itself.

Return an encoded text of minimum length that decodes back to `s`, following these rules:

- A block may be used only where its written form is strictly shorter than the letters it decodes to, so a string that cannot be shortened is returned unchanged (for example `"aaaa"` stays `"aaaa"`, not `"4[a]"`).
- When several encodings reach the minimum length, any one of them is accepted.
constraints: s consists only of lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

The best encoding of any piece of `s` is built from best encodings of smaller pieces: a piece is either written as is, cut into two parts encoded separately, or, when it is a whole number of copies of a shorter unit, written as `count[unit]` with the unit encoded as well as possible. That makes this an interval DP over all substrings, filled from short to long. Trying every cut and every unit length by recursion works too, but the DP keeps it to O(n³) with a fast repeat test.

## Approach

1. Let `dp[i][j]` be the shortest encoding of `s[i..j]`. Fill it by increasing `length`.
2. Start each entry as the plain substring `sub`. Pieces shorter than 5 letters can never be shortened, so stop there for them.
3. Try every `split`: `dp[i][split] + dp[split + 1][j]` replaces the entry when it is strictly shorter.
4. Find the smallest `period` of `sub` with `(sub + sub).indexOf(sub, 1)`. If it is less than `length`, `sub` is `length / period` copies of its first `period` letters, so `packed` = count `[` best unit `]` is a candidate.
5. Keep `packed` only when it is strictly shorter, and return `dp[0][n - 1]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "aaa"`, so `n = 3`. Every substring has `length` below 5, so each `dp[i][j]` is just `sub`: `"a"`, then `"aa"`, then `dp[0][2] = "aaa"`, which is returned. For comparison, with `"aaaaa"` the full piece has `period = 1`, so `packed = "5[a]"`, one letter shorter than the plain text.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n³): O(n²) substrings, each with O(n) splits and an O(n) repeat test (string building adds a factor bounded by the encoding lengths).
- Space: O(n³) characters in the worst case for the stored encodings, O(n²) entries.

## Pitfalls

- Replace only on a strictly shorter candidate; `"aaaa"` must stay `"aaaa"`, since `"4[a]"` saves nothing.
- Encode the repeated unit with `dp`, not as raw text, so nested blocks such as `2[2[abbb]c]` are found.
- The count can have two or three digits (`150[a]`); measure the real text, not a fixed overhead.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dp[i][j]` | shortest encoding found for `s[i..j]` |
| `length`, `i`, `j` | size and ends of the current substring |
| `sub` | the substring itself |
| `split` | last index of the left part in a cut |
| `joined` | encoding made by joining the two parts |
| `period` | length of the smallest unit that tiles `sub` |
| `packed` | the `count[unit]` candidate |
